definition: dwell unhappily on a thought; also a group of young birds
memoryTip: Like a hen brooding — sit and stew on dark thoughts (or a clutch of chicks).
correctPassage: He tended to brood over mistakes long after others had moved on.
wrongPassages: She brooded the good news by throwing a party the same night.
He brooded over the joke for two seconds, then forgot it entirely.
They brood cheerfully whenever a hard problem finally gets solved.

definition: deep respect, often tinged with awe
memoryTip: Revere someone — treat them with deep, almost sacred respect.
correctPassage: The ceremony was conducted with quiet reverence for those lost.
wrongPassages: He showed reverence for the archive by doodling in the margins of every page.
Their reverence for the coach was clear when they ignored every instruction.
She treated the heirloom with reverence by leaving it in a damp garage.

definition: serving as a desirable model; outstandingly good
memoryTip: Worthy to be an example — model behavior others should copy.
correctPassage: Her laboratory notebooks are exemplary in their clarity and care.
wrongPassages: His exemplary manners included cutting off every speaker mid-sentence.
The exemplary report mixed up names, dates, and half the figures.
They called the empty attendance sheet exemplary of a thriving program.

definition: openly resist or refuse to obey; go against
memoryTip: De-fy: refuse to bow — openly resist an order or expectation.
correctPassage: The results appear to defy the predictions of the standard model.
wrongPassages: She chose to defy the curfew by arriving home an hour early every night.
The class decided to defy the teacher by copying the notes word for word as instructed.
He managed to defy the ban by carefully following every rule on the list.

definition: important or relevant (as in material evidence)
memoryTip: Matters materially — important/relevant, not just “stuff” you can touch.
correctPassage: Only material differences between the samples were reported in the abstract.
wrongPassages: The typo was material to the verdict and changed nothing about the case.
A material clue would be one the jury could safely ignore.
She called the blank footnote material because it added zero evidence.

definition: ability to stretch and resume shape; adaptability
memoryTip: Like elastic — stretches and snaps back; also flexible response to change.
correctPassage: The market showed surprising elasticity in response to the price change.
wrongPassages: Glass is prized for its elasticity when it shatters at the lightest tap.
The schedule’s elasticity meant every hour was locked and nonnegotiable.
His elasticity of mind rejected every new idea without a second look.

definition: a scarcity or lack of something
memoryTip: Sounds like “death of supply” — a serious lack or shortage.
correctPassage: A dearth of qualified applicants delayed the hire for months.
wrongPassages: A dearth of volunteers filled every shift twice over.
They celebrated the dearth of rain that flooded the valley for days.
The pantry’s dearth of snacks left shelves stacked to the ceiling.

definition: make something seem less important than it is
memoryTip: Play it down — shrink how big or serious something sounds.
correctPassage: Officials tried to downplay the severity of the shortage.
wrongPassages: She downplayed the award by hosting a city-wide parade in her honor.
They downplayed the risk by printing warnings in foot-high red type.
He downplayed the scandal by leaking every detail to the evening news.

definition: surpass; go beyond or move faster than
memoryTip: Strip ahead of the pack — run past and leave others behind.
correctPassage: Demand continues to outstrip the region’s ability to supply housing.
wrongPassages: Sales outstripped the forecast by falling short every single quarter.
Her pace outstripped the field when she finished dead last.
New hires outstripped veterans by needing twice as much coaching.

definition: tendency to stay unchanged; resistance to a change in motion
memoryTip: Newton’s inertia — stays still (or keeps going) until something pushes it.
correctPassage: Institutional inertia made reforming the curriculum slow and difficult.
wrongPassages: The startup’s inertia was famous for reinventing its product every week.
Her inertia showed when she rewrote the plan three times before lunch.
Market inertia meant prices flipped with every rumor by noon.
